author: rana-abdalla
description: Every answer from an AI comes out of a building full of machines running day and night. How much electricity does it really take, from training the model to the grid that powers it?

hero.hook: AI looks like software, but every answer is made in a very real building, plugged into the same grid as your home.

blocks.text: You ask an online AI a question, and the answer appears within seconds. The work itself does not happen in your phone. It happens in a [[data center]], a building full of machines that process and store information. Those machines draw electricity around the clock, even though nobody ever sees them.

In 2025, according to the [[International Energy Agency]], all data centers together used about **1.5%** of the world's electricity. That figure covers every kind of online service, not AI alone. But facilities built for AI are multiplying fast. A short reply costs little on its own. Yet machines still run for every one of them, and several systems draw power at the same time to produce it.

A [[server]] is a computer that handles data and runs online services. In a data center, servers do most of the computing, which makes them the biggest electricity users. Split up the bill of a modern data center and servers take about **60%** of it on average. That figure describes data centers in general, not AI facilities alone.

blocks.caption: Rows of servers in a data center: they are the ones that use most of the electricity.

blocks.text: The rest goes to storing and moving data, cooling the equipment and keeping the building running. Cooling matters because a computer gives off heat while it works. Without a system to remove it, the machines would end up overheating. The electricity behind an AI answer therefore powers far more than the computers producing it.
According to the IEA, electricity consumption in AI-focused data centers grew by 50% in 2025 alone.

Before it can answer, an AI service needs a model: a system that has learned patterns from examples. Creating it takes [[training]], a phase in which computers work through enormous amounts of data. That work can keep very powerful machines busy for long stretches.

blocks.caption: The cabinets of NASA's Columbia supercomputer: the kind of machine used to train a model.

blocks.text: Once the model is trained, another kind of work begins. This is [[inference]], the computation that produces a response to your request. Training does not start over in full with every question; inference, on the other hand, happens again for each request. Which of the two weighs more over time? That depends on how the service is built and how many people use it. A busy service keeps its computers answering, even between two major rounds of training.

How much electricity does a single text request use? Published estimates do not give the same answer. Google, measuring its live service, puts its median text request at **0.24 Wh**. The [[watt-hour]] (Wh) is the unit used to measure an amount of energy. A separate study arrives at a median of **0.31 Wh**, with the middle half of its standard requests falling between **0.16 and 0.60 Wh**.

These figures do not contradict each other: they describe different systems and methods, not two opposing measurements of the same task. They also leave out much heavier jobs. Asking an AI to reason through several steps before answering keeps its computers busy far longer. The energy per request therefore depends on the system, on how it is measured and on the work being asked.
In the same study, a long reasoning request, where the model works through its steps before concluding, reaches a median of 3.91 Wh, more than ten times a standard request.

sections.title: One request has no fixed cost

blocks.text: The [[electricity grid]] is the network of lines that carries power from generating plants to homes and businesses. Large AI facilities plug into that same network. To give a sense of scale, the IEA compares the annual electricity use of a typical AI-focused data center, a facility built mainly to run these services, with that of about **100,000 households**.

blocks.caption: Pylons of a 750 kV high-voltage line: data centers plug into this same grid.

blocks.text: These facilities also tend to cluster in the same places. When several large sites need power in the same area, they share the local network, and the existing lines may need upgrading. A region with spare capacity can take in new sites more easily than one already close to its limits. Where AI infrastructure is built therefore makes a difference to its neighbors.
AI's electricity is spent on several levels, from the servers that need cooling to the local grid, and the cost of one request depends on the system, the measurement and the work being asked.
